postTitle: Unmarried Couples: Building the Protections Marriage Gives
topic: Marriage switches on a bundle of defaults; living together switches on almost none

assumptions.notes: No figures. From the post: marriage usually switches on inheritance without a will, survivor pension benefits, medical decision rights, joint or favourable tax, low tax gifts and inheritance between spouses, a property regime, a separation framework and a residency route. Unmarried partners usually get none of these by default in most places. Common law marriage does not exist in most places; England and Wales have no such status; Australia, New Zealand and several Canadian provinces give rights after a qualifying period. Five documents rebuild most of it: a will, beneficiary designations, how the home is owned, a cohabitation agreement, powers of attorney. Tax treatment usually cannot be rebuilt. Rules vary by country. Not legal advice.

caption.instagram:
Together for years, not married? In many places, the law can treat your partner as a stranger.

Marriage switches on a bundle of financial defaults the day you sign: inheritance without a will, medical decisions, a legal regime for shared property, often joint tax. Living together may create no automatic inheritance or decision rights, however long you have been together. Common law marriage is widely believed in and rarely exists, though some countries do give rights after a qualifying period.

Written records can make the household's intentions visible: a will, a record of how you own your home, a cohabitation agreement and powers of attorney. With beneficiary forms, five documents rebuild most of the bundle. Tax is the row they usually cannot fix.
